2.2.4 YEAST Systematic Position Kingdom Division Class Order Family Genus
: Mycota : Ascomycota : Saccharomycetes : Saccharomycetales : Saccharomycetaceae : Saccharomyces

Occurrence They are saprophytic fungi and are cosmopolitan in distribution. They grow on rotting fruits, cane juice, nectaries of flowers, sweets, decaying organic matter and milk products. Some yeast grows as parasites on plants and animals (e.g. Candida albicans).

Morphology Yeast is non-mycelial unicellular fungi having oval or spherical cell. Sometimes, the yeast may form branched or unbranched temporary chain of up to 100 cells and this is known as pseudomycelium. Cell wall of each cell is thin, delicate and made of chitin. Cell membrane lies inner to cell wall. The cytoplasm is containing the cell organelles like mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi bodies, ribosome, and reserve food materials in the form of glycogen or fats. A large central vacuole surrounded by the membrane, tonoplast is present. Nucleus is attached at one end of a large central vacuole. Such type of vacuole is called nuclear vacuole.

Figure 2.4.10 Structure of Yeast cell Reproduction Yeast reproduces by vegetative and sexual method. 1. Vegetative method: Vegetative method in yeast takes place during favourable condition. It takes place by budding and fission method. a. By budding: It is the common method of reproduction in yeast, takes place during favourable condition i.e. in sugar solution.

Figure 2.4.11 Budding in Yeast During this process, a small bud like out growth appears at one end of the parent cell which gradually enlarges in size. The nucleus enlarges and divides amitotically into two daughter nuclei. One nucleus along with other cytoplasmic contents passes into the bud and the other remains in the parent cell. The vacuole almost disappears at this stage. Gradually the bud becomes almost of the same size as the parent cell. Wall formation occurs between the bud and mother cell. Then the bud behaves as a new individual. During rapid growth, the daughter cell also gives bud while still attached to the mother cell, this form false mycelium known as pseudomycelium. b. By fission: During this process, a somatic cell of yeast enlarges in size and its nucleus is divided into two daughter nuclei. Then a partition wall is formed at the middle of the cell dividing the parent protoplasm into two halves each having one nucleus. These halves then separate into two cells and lead an independent life.

Figure 2.4.12 Fission in yeast 2. Sexual Reproduction: It takes place during unfavorable condition. The sex organs are not formed in yeast and the sexual fusion occurs between two vegetative cells of opposite mating type, which behave as gametangia. It is known as conjugation. Depending upon the prominence of haploid or diploid phase, the sexual life cycle of yeast is of following types: a. Haplobiontic life cycle: This type of sexual life cycle occurs in Schizosaccharomyces octosporus. In this type of life cycle, the haploid phase is dominant than diploid phase.

Figure 2.4.13 Haplobiontic life cycle of yeast Two haploid cells of opposite strain come together and behave as gametangia. They develop an outgrowth toward each other and come in contact with each other. The contact wall dissolves and forms conjugation tube. The nuclei of two gametangia in the tube fuse to form a diploid zygote. The zygote grows and acts as an ascus. The diploid nucleus divides meiotically to form four haploid nuclei which further divide mitotically to form eight nuclei. Each nucleus develops into an ascospore within the ascus. After maturity, the wall of the ascus ruptures and the ascospores are liberated and act as haploid, uninucleate independent vegetative cell of yeast. b. Diplobiontic life cycle: This type of sexual life cycle occurs in Saccharomyces ludwigii. In this type of life cycle, the diploid phase is dominant than haploid phase.

During unfavourable condition, the diploid somatic cell directly behaves as ascus. The nucleus undergoes meiotic cell division to form four haploid somatic nuclei of two mating type Biology, Grade 11 | 97

that develop into four ascospores. The ascospores of the opposite matting types undergo conjugation inside the ascus. The zygote cell formed within the ascus develops a germ tube. The germ tubes break the ascus wall and form a ‘sprout mycelium’. The sprout mycelium produces several diploid somatic cells.

Figure 2.4.14 Diplobiontic life cycle of yeast c. Haplodiplobiontic life cycle: This type of sexual life cycle occurs in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In this type of life cycle, both haploid and diploid phases are equally dominant in the life cycle.
